# RATIÉ CH. 5 — WHAT ŚAIVA AND BUDDHIST IDEALISM SHARE
*Per-chapter analysis for the thesis. Source lines 14549–17193. The common-ground finding:
Śaiva and Buddhist idealism both hold consciousness-fundamental; they diverge on the nature
of the subject.*

---

## 1. THE CHAPTER'S THESIS
The Pratyabhijñā shares its starting point with the Vijñānavāda (Buddhist idealism):
both hold the object is an aspect (ākāra) of cognition and consciousness is fundamental.
The divergence: the Pratyabhijñā adds a *permanent, unifying subject* — the self that
recognition discloses.

## 2. EXTENDED QUOTES (French verbatim + English translation)

### Q1 — The two idealisms share the consciousness-fundamental ground (lines 14596–14601)
> "les arguments qui s'y trouvent développés pourraient sans difficulté être attribués à
> quelque vijñānavādin, et la proximité de l'idéalisme bouddhique et de celui de la
> Pratyabhijñā se manifeste ici avec la plus grande évidence."
> **"the arguments developed here could without difficulty be attributed to some
> Vijñānavādin, and the proximity of Buddhist idealism to that of the Pratyabhijñā manifests
> itself here with the greatest evidence."**

### Q2 — The object must be light (prakāśa) — consciousness-fundamental (ĪPK 1.5.2, lines 14736–14745)
> "les objets, pour pouvoir être manifestés, doivent avoir pour nature prakāśa… l'essence
> (ātman) de l'objet, c'est d'être lumière consciente (prakāśatā)."
> **"objects, to be manifested, must have prakāśa as their nature… the essence (ātman) of
> the object is to be conscious light (prakāśatā)."**

### Q3 — Perception as the experience of otherness (aham/idam) (lines 14779–14817)
> "percevoir, c'est faire l'expérience fondamentale de l'altérité… une entité qui ne se
> laisse pas réduire au Je (aham), mais s'impose comme un ceci (idam)… séparé (bhinna) du
> sujet."
> **"to perceive is to undergo the fundamental experience of otherness… an entity that does
> not allow itself to be reduced to the 'I' (aham), but imposes itself as a 'this' (idam)…
> separate (bhinna) from the subject."**

**→** The datum the thesis must reinterpret: perception *feels* like otherness (aham/idam
split). Recognition re-renders this as self.

### Q4 — The object's Self is consciousness; the mirror/reflection identity (lines 14911–14929, 15340–15360)
> "tout objet manifesté par la conscience a pour 'Soi' ou pour 'essence' (ātman) la
> conscience… Il y a donc une identité (tādātmya) foncière du reflet et du miroir, et cette
> identité est la condition de possibilité du reflet – hors du miroir, le reflet n'est rien."
> **"every object manifested by consciousness has consciousness for its 'Self' or 'essence'
> (ātman)… There is therefore a fundamental identity (tādātmya) of the reflection and the
> mirror, and this identity is the condition of possibility of the reflection — outside the
> mirror, the reflection is nothing."**

**→ THE THESIS NODE.** The object is *re-cognized* as one's own luminous self (tādātmya) —
the felt structure of recognition.

### Q5 — Shared ground + the divergence (lines 15943–16043)
> "de ce point de vue, la Pratyabhijñā ne dit pas autre chose que le Vijñānavāda… [mais] la
> doctrine selon laquelle l'objet n'est qu'un aspect de la cognition implique que la
> conscience est davantage qu'une série hétérogène de cognitions instantanées."
> **"from this point of view, the Pratyabhijñā says nothing other than the Vijñānavāda…
> [but] the doctrine that the object is only an aspect of cognition implies that
> consciousness is more than a heterogeneous series of instantaneous cognitions."**

**→ THE HINGE.** The shared ākāra thesis *implies* a permanent unifying consciousness — the
self that recognition discloses.

### Q6 — The un-recognized principle is the root of error (lines 17186–17191)
> "Les objets… ne sont pas svaniṣṭhita… Tant que ce principe n'est pas reconnu, ce n'est pas
> seulement la mémoire ou l'identité personnelle, mais encore la possibilité même de toute
> perception, qui reste incompréhensible."
> **"Objects… are not svaniṣṭhita… So long as this principle is not recognized, it is not
> only memory or personal identity, but even the very possibility of all perception, that
> remains incomprehensible."**

**→ THE THESIS.** Not recognizing the consciousness-fundamental = the root of all error.
Recognition (pratyabhijñā) is precisely this re-cognition of the self.

## 3. IPK LINKS
- **ĪPK 1.5.1–1.5.3** — the object must be within / be light (the consciousness-fundamental
  claim). Q2, Q3, Q4.
- **ĪPK 1.5.3** — sākāra cognition (differentiation of consciousness, via Dharmakīrti).
- **ĪPK 1.3.6–1.3.7** — the permanent subject / unifier implied by the ākāra thesis.

## 4. THESIS LITERATURE-REVIEW VALUE
- **The common-ground finding** (Q1, Q5): Śaiva recognition is not naive realism — it
  shares consciousness-fundamental with the Buddhist idealism it transforms. The Stage 1
  "common-ground" scholarly gold.
- **Consciousness-fundamental** (Q2, Q6): everything real is light; the un-recognized
  principle = root of error. The paper's Part III (mind is fundamental).
- **The object as self** (Q4): tādātmya (identity) of reflection and mirror = the felt
  structure of recognition — the object re-cognized as one's own luminous self.
- **Perception-as-otherness** (Q3): the aham/idam split is what recognition re-renders.

## 5. IPVV TRANSLATION HOOKS
- **ākāra / ābhāsa** (aspect / manifestation) — the shared cognition-structure.
- **prakāśa / prakāśatā** (light / being-light) — consciousness-fundamental.
- **tādātmya** (identity) — reflection and mirror.
- **svaniṣṭhita** (resting in oneself) — what objects are NOT.
- **aham / idam** (I / this) — the felt split recognition re-renders.
- **anubhava** (experience) — the felt character of cognition.

---
*Ch5 is the common-ground chapter: Śaiva and Buddhist idealism share consciousness-
fundamental (Q1, Q2), and the shared ākāra thesis implies a permanent subject (Q5). The
object is re-cognized as one's own luminous self (Q4, tādātmya). Not-recognizing this is
the root of error (Q6). This is the paper's Stage 1 common-ground + consciousness-fundamental
foundation.*
